newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals - Cobalt set to rise on small US sales.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals - Cobalt set to rise on small US sales.

text.p: Cobalt prices are set to rise after the summer holidays, with lower-than expected sales of U.S. stockpiles adding to tightness in the market caused by lower production in Africa, traders said on Tuesday.
"The prices are set to rise after the summer holidays," said a trader at one of Japan's major trading houses. "Neither users nor producers have that much stock."
Traders said a plan by the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center to sell another 500,000 lbs of cobalt by the end of September has failed to allay worries over further price rises.
The amount was much smaller than the market's expectation of about 1.5 million lbs at the next auction, putting additional pressure on prices, they said.
Many traders said the price for high-grade cobalt would edge up towards $25 per pound from $22.50-23.00 while the price for low-grade cobalt would rise towards $21 from $19.40-20.00.

A strike at Falconbridge Ltd's Sudbury plant since August 1 has put psychological pressure on metal prices, although the strike may end shortly as the union said on Monday it and the firm were close to an agreement, they added.
One trader calculated the world's cobalt supply would total 24,950 tonnes this year, including 3,400 tonnes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire, and 3,500 tonnes from Zambia.
This would be below total demand of 25,500 tonnes, which includes Japan's demand of about 6,500 tonnes, he said.
In the magnesium market, the price for Chinese metal was unchanged at $2,450/$2,500 per tonne, traders said.
However, they said they were carefully watching the outcome of dumping charges against Chinese magnesium in Europe, with a decision expected as early as later this month.

"Depending on the results, the prices might come down a bit," said one magnesium trader. But he said the downside was limited as there were no longer Chinese producers willing to sell the metal for low prices.
Traders said tough negotiations over the price for Dead Sea magnesium were continuing, with Japanese users reluctant to accept high prices offered by the Western producer.
Ferro-vanadium prices rose further, with some small lot deals seen struck at a price of above $20 per kg. Molybdenum oxide, on the other hand, was flat at $4.40/4.60 per pound, traders said.
One trader said: "European (vanadium) converters are resuming their operations after the summer holidays. But Belgium converters seem to be shut down due to some trouble."
In China, the minor metals market presented a mixed picture as summer holidays in Europe wound down and traders trickled back to work, sources in Hong Kong and China said.
Chinese magnesium prices were heard quoted between a range of US$2,360 and $2,400 per tonne, FOB China.
At least one China-based trader said inquiries had been steady and that domestic Chinese prices were edging up slowly.
Cobalt was picking up slightly, with one source reporting about 25 tonnes sold to China over the past week. This could not be confirmed.
"If the market moves up slightly, the Chinese buying is very good," the source said.
Chinese cobalt offers were heard at $20.50-$21.50, CIF Hong Kong. Russian-origin cobalt was seen cheaper, at $19.80-$20.00 per lb for prompt release in Hong Kong.
Silicon's situation was mixed too, with supplies seen currently healthy, offers plentiful and ranging between $900 per tonne and $950 per tonne, FOB China.
"I'm a bit confused (about the price), the supplies are quite good," said one trader in South China.
Traders said that some factories had shifted production into low gear and that demand was not particularly healthy.

"I think silicon prices are at the bottom now," said one trader, noting they may go up in another month or so and that material had been booked in August with Chinese producers at $900 and $910 per tonne.
In ferro-vanadium, raw material tightness in China meant production was being dampened, traders said. They noted that only limited quantities were available from South Africa.
In China's Sichuan province, some ferro-vanadium was being produced, but the amounts were small, one source said.
Chinese offers hovered around $19.80 and $19.85 per kg, traders said, but declined to estimate whether prices would cross $20 per kg.
